## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89131.4.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89131.4.sa3)

I remain enthusiastic about this study. The manuscript is well-written, logical, and conceptually clear. To my knowledge, no prior modeling study has tackled the question of 'why prepare before executing, why not just execute?' Prior studies have simply assumed, to emulate empirical findings, that preparatory inputs precede execution. They never asked why. The authors show that, when there are constraints on inputs, preparation becomes a natural strategy. In contrast, with no constraint on inputs, there is no need for preparation as one could get anything one liked just via the inputs during movement. For the sake of tractability, the authors use a simple magnitude constraint: the cost function punishes the integral of the squared inputs. Thus, if small inputs before movement can reduce the size of the inputs needed during movement, preparation is a good strategy. This occurs if (and only if) the network has strong dynamics (otherwise feeding it preparatory activity would not produce anything interesting). All of this is sensible and clarifying.

As discussed in the prior round of reviews, the central constraint that the authors use is a mathematically tractable stand-in for a range of plausible (but often trickier to define and evaluate) constraints, such as simplicity of inputs (or inputs being things that other areas could provide). The manuscript now embraces this fact more explicitly and also gives some results showing that other constraints (such as on the derivative of activity, which is one component of complexity) can have the same effect. The manuscript also now discusses and addresses a modest weakness of the previous manuscript: the preparatory activity in their simulations is often overly complex temporally, lacking the (rough) plateau typically seen for data. Depending on your point of view, this is simply 'window dressing', but from my perspective it was important to know that their approach could yield more realistic-looking preparatory activity.

The most recent version of the manuscript also has a useful section in the Discussion on the topic of preparation when there is no external delay, which I found helpful given prior behavioral and physiological studies arguing that preparation can (1) be very brief, but (2) is always present. These findings mesh nicely with the authors' central result that preparation is a good network strategy, and that it would thus be normative for there to be at least a brief interval of preparation even when not imposed externally.

results.result: Prior work has established that motor areas display movement-specific preparatory activity before movement onset, which has been proposed to seed initial neural states. Recent experiments have also revealed the presence and necessity of ongoing inputs during movement, including critical pattern-generating input from the thalamus.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C3, C8, and C9 accurately summarize established findings from prior experimental work, supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide the empirical and theoretical context for the current study and are well-documented in the literature.

results.result: In an optimally controlled inhibition-stabilized network model of M1, delay-period inputs consistently arise before movement onset. Network activity begins changing well before the go cue, driven by early inputs that cancel in the readout to keep the hand still. The preparation index plateaus at ~1.3 for delays >300 ms, with preparation enabling faster reaches and reducing control effort.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C20, C27-C30, C33-C36 describe the main findings from the optimal control modeling (Figures 2-3). The results are internally consistent and supported by the presented data showing preparatory inputs, preparation index dynamics, and cost function components. The modeling framework and results are clearly documented.

results.result: When preparation time exceeds ~300 ms, the optimal controller does not utilize the additional early time. Instead, external inputs continue to arise just a couple hundred milliseconds before movement initiation, with firing rates and PCA trajectories remaining similar across different delay periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 describe findings from Figure 3 showing that preparation timing is constrained by network timescales. The data clearly demonstrate that longer delays do not lead to earlier preparation, supporting the interpretation that network dynamics have characteristic timescales that limit the utility of very early inputs.

results.result: In simplified 2D networks with nonnormal or oscillatory dynamics, optimal control generally produces preparatory inputs, but the amount depends critically on readout orientation. In nonnormal networks, reading out the sink mode yields lower cost and more preparation than reading out the source mode. In oscillatory networks, preparation is independent of readout direction but consistently moves activity along the output-null axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50, C52 describe systematic analyses of 2D networks (Figure 4) that isolate the effects of specific dynamical motifs. The results are clearly presented and logically consistent, demonstrating how network structure and readout geometry interact to determine optimal preparation strategies.

results.result: Two control-theoretic quantities—observability of the nullspace (α) and controllability of the readout (β)—largely explain preparation in networks. For preparation to be beneficial, the nullspace must be sufficiently observable and the readout must have limited controllability. These quantities predict preparation across diverse network architectures.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C53-C56 present the theoretical framework linking network properties to preparation (Figure 5). The linear regression achieves R²=0.93 for ISNs and R²=0.69 for other network types, providing strong quantitative support. The control-theoretic formalization is mathematically sound and generalizes across network families.

results.result: Optimal control of sequential reaches produces two phases of preparation, one before each movement, consistent with experimental observations in monkeys. In the model, this arises because the network's limited timescales require reinjection of inputs to produce the transient activity growth needed for the second reach after the hand stops at the first target.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C63-C69 describe modeling of sequential reaches (Figure 6) that reproduces key experimental findings from Zimnik and Churchland (2021). The preparatory subspace analysis shows two clear peaks of occupancy before each reach, and the mechanistic explanation based on network timescales is logically consistent with the model's dynamics.

results.result: Most published network models of delayed reaches can perform the task equally well without preparatory inputs, with inputs confined to the movement epoch.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is demonstrated by the authors' own modeling (Figure 1B) showing that the same reach can be produced with movement-only inputs. This observation motivates the central question of the paper and is clearly illustrated.

results.result: Prior theoretical and modeling work has established that motor cortex operates as a dynamical system with near-autonomous evolution during movement, that preparation benefits behavior and may facilitate learning, and that previous models typically assume preparatory inputs by design.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C11-C17 accurately summarize established theoretical frameworks and prior modeling approaches, supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for understanding the novelty of the current approach, which does not assume preparatory inputs a priori.

results.result: The authors modeled M1 as an input-driven RNN coupled to a two-link arm model, using iLQR to find optimal control inputs that minimize a cost functional. They employed inhibition-stabilized networks previously shown to capture M1 dynamics, with reaches required within 600 ms of a go cue following a known delay period.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C23, C74-C78, C80 describe the methodological framework. The approach is clearly documented with appropriate citations to established methods (Li and Todorov 2004, Hennequin et al. 2014). The iLQR algorithm is appropriate for this nonlinear optimal control problem.

results.result: Preparatory neural activity patterns arise from optimal control of reaching movements at the level of motor cortical circuits, providing a normative explanation for experimental findings.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 represents the main conclusion of the study, which is well-supported by the comprehensive modeling results (C4, C20-C22, C27-C40, C44-C56, C63-C69). The optimal control framework successfully reproduces key experimental observations and provides mechanistic insights into why preparation emerges.

results.result: Networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons embed two main connectivity motifs: feedforward (nonnormal) connectivity and anti-symmetric connectivity causing oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 accurately describes established knowledge about E-I network dynamics, appropriately cited. This provides the theoretical basis for the 2D network analyses in Figure 4.

results.result: Zimnik and Churchland (2021) concluded that each reach in a sequence is successively seeded by its own preparatory activity rather than the whole sequence unrolling from a single preparatory period.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 accurately summarizes the key finding from the cited experimental study, providing the empirical motivation for the sequential reach modeling in Figure 6.

results.result: The experimental data shown in Figure 1 came from two monkeys trained on delayed reaching tasks, with recordings from PMd and M1 using 96-electrode arrays, under protocols approved by Stanford IACUC.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 describe the source of experimental data used for comparison. These are factual statements about previously published datasets with appropriate citations to the original studies.

results.result: In an optimally controlled inhibition-stabilized network model of M1, delay-period inputs consistently arise well before movement begins. Network activity changes before the go cue, driven by early inputs that cancel in the readout to keep the hand still. The preparation index plateaus at ~1.3 for delays >300 ms, and preparation changes the optimal control strategy, improving task performance.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'report that when there is a cost on the inputs, the optimal inputs should start before the desired network output.' Reviewer 2 notes 'They show that networks optimised under reasonable constraints...will use the input to seed the state of the network before movement.' Reviewer 4 confirms 'the authors show that, when there are constraints on inputs, preparation becomes a natural strategy.'

results.result: With varying delay periods, the optimal controller makes little use of preparation time beyond ~300 ms before the go cue. External inputs continue to arise just a couple hundred milliseconds before movement initiation regardless of longer preparation times, and single neuron firing rates and PCA trajectories remain remarkably similar across different delay periods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 4 notes the manuscript 'has a useful section in the Discussion on the topic of preparation when there is no external delay' and that 'preparation can (1) be very brief, but (2) is always present,' which aligns with these timing results. No reviewer questions the delay period analysis.

results.result: Preparation can be largely explained by two control-theoretic quantities: observability of the readout's nullspace (α) and limited controllability of the readout (β). For a network to benefit from preparation, there must exist output-null activity patterns that seed output-potent dynamics, the nullspace must be sufficiently observable, and there must be sizeable cost to input-driven movement without preparation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms this theoretical contribution: 'they identify a strong connection between the structure of the network and the amount of preparation that is optimal for control - namely, that preparation has the most value when nullspaces are highly observable relative to the readout dimension and when the controllability of readout dimensions is low.' No reviewer challenges this mechanistic explanation.

results.result: In simplified 2-unit networks with feedforward (nonnormal) and oscillatory motifs, optimal control generally leads to preparatory dynamics. In the feedforward motif, preparation depends critically on readout orientation—reading out the sink mode yields lower cost and more preparation than reading out the source mode. In the oscillatory network, the controller consistently moves activity along the output-null axis during preparation to engage rotational flow after the go cue.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 affirms the authors 'present compelling evidence by combining mathematically tractable analyses in linear networks and numerical simulation in nonlinear networks.' Reviewer 3 praises 'the mechanisms by which it happens by dissecting in detail low-dimensional networks.' No reviewer questions these simplified network analyses.

results.result: Optimal control of compound reaches leads to input-driven preparatory activity in a dedicated subspace prior to each movement, consistent with experimental findings. For double reaches with pauses, the preparatory subspace is occupied twice; for compound reaches without pauses, occupancy rises before the first movement, decays slightly, then peaks again before the second reach. This arises from the requirement that the hand stop briefly at the first target, necessitating activity re-growth via input reinjection.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes the model 'predictions are consistent with the observation in monkey motor cortex' regarding sequential preparation. However, Reviewer 3 identifies significant discrepancies: 'the data reproduced from Zimnik and Churchland show preparatory inputs that have a very asymmetric shape that really plummets before the start of the next movement, whereas the derived inputs have larger amplitude during the movement period.' Reviewer 3 also notes differences in trigger signals and correlation patterns between conditions, suggesting only partial consistency with data.

results.result: Most published network models of delayed reaches can perform the task just as well without preparatory inputs, with external inputs confined to the movement epoch, as demonstrated in Figure 1B.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly confirms this motivation: 'Prior studies have simply assumed, to emulate empirical findings, that preparatory inputs precede execution. They never asked why.' This validates the authors' demonstration that previous models don't require preparation, establishing the novelty of the current work's approach.

results.result: The authors modeled motor cortex as an input-driven dynamical system using an inhibition-stabilized network coupled to a model arm, and used the iLQR algorithm to find optimal spatiotemporal input patterns that minimize a cost functional combining target accuracy and input effort.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 affirms the approach 'provides valuable theoretical insight' and that 'treating input to motor cortex as a signal that is optimised directly...is able to sidestep many...problematic questions.' However, Reviewer 3 raises significant methodological concerns: 'iLQR...has a limited ability to leverage potential advantages of nonlinearities' and 'is not a biologically plausible learning rule,' noting this 'can confound the question of whether [differences] come from a difference of assumed objective or a difference of optimization procedure.' Reviewer 4 acknowledges the 'simple magnitude constraint' is 'a mathematically tractable stand-in for a range of plausible...constraints.'

results.result: The decrease in target cost with preparation was due to the model producing faster reaches, while the decrease in effort cost arose from smaller control inputs being necessary when preparation was allowed.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 summarizes this mechanism: 'if small inputs before movement can reduce the size of the inputs needed during movement, preparation is a good strategy. This occurs if (and only if) the network has strong dynamics.' No reviewer challenges this explanation of the cost reduction.

results.result: Preparatory neural activity patterns arise from optimal control of reaching movements at the level of motor cortical circuits, providing a possible explanation for observed experimental findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 calls this 'an important study' that 'provides a new perspective on why preparatory activity occurs.' Reviewer 2 states it 'provides valuable theoretical insight into the role of preparation.' However, Reviewer 3 extensively discusses limitations, noting the framework 'cannot easily account for some other varied types of objectives' such as 'reusability of parts of the circuit, sparse use of additional neurons...and ease of planning.' Reviewer 3 also questions whether the model can explain preparation in 'more sensory-feedback-driven' movements and notes that 'some M1 properties that lead to strong preparation...may not be favorable for control in general.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C37-C40 regarding preparation timing constraints from network timescales. Both evaluations find these claims supported by the data, with peer reviewers noting the manuscript's useful discussion of preparation timing.

Perfect agreement on claims C44-C50, C52 regarding 2D network analyses. Both evaluations support these findings, with peer reviewers praising the mathematically tractable analyses and detailed dissection of low-dimensional networks.

Perfect agreement on claims C21, C53-C56 regarding the theoretical framework linking network properties to preparation. Both evaluations support the mechanistic explanation, with peer reviewers explicitly affirming the connection between network structure and optimal preparation.

Perfect agreement on claim C10 demonstrating that movement can be produced without preparatory inputs. Both evaluations support this as valid motivation for the study, with peer reviewers confirming this establishes the novelty of asking why preparation occurs.

Divergent evaluations on claim C70 (main conclusion). OpenEval finds it well-supported by comprehensive modeling results. Peer reviewers acknowledge valuable theoretical insight but express uncertainty due to limitations in accounting for other objectives, applicability to feedback-driven movements, and questions about generalizability.

Strong agreement on claims C4, C20, C27-C30, C35-C36 regarding core findings from optimal control modeling. Both evaluations support these claims, with all peer reviewers explicitly affirming that preparation emerges naturally under input constraints.

Divergent evaluations on claims C22, C63-C69 regarding sequential reach modeling. OpenEval finds claims supported with clear reproduction of experimental findings. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting consistency with some observations but identifying significant discrepancies in input shape, timing, and correlation patterns compared to actual data.

Divergent evaluations on claims C18-C19, C75-C77 regarding methodological framework. OpenEval finds the approach clearly documented and appropriate. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, acknowledging theoretical value but raising concerns about iLQR's limited ability to leverage nonlinearities, biological implausibility, and potential confounding of objectives with optimization procedures.

Agreement on claims C33-C34 regarding cost reduction mechanism. OpenEval supports these as part of broader modeling findings. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this mechanism, noting that preparation reduces input costs when networks have strong dynamics.

Both address claim C62 (experimental finding from Zimnik and Churchland). OpenEval finds it accurately summarizes the cited study. Peer reviewers note consistency with some observations but identify discrepancies in the model's reproduction of these findings.
OpenEval finds claims C1-C3, C8-C9 (established findings from prior work) well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval finds claims C6-C7, C11-C17 (theoretical frameworks and prior modeling approaches) accurately summarize established work with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.
OpenEval finds claim C43 (E-I network dynamics) accurately describes established knowledge with appropriate citation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this background claim.
